Actually LISTEN to your people and understand what people do if you want to keep customers.   

You can't ask executives any question. We used to have great bosses who were all about open chats and teamwork. But now? Decisions are made in secret, zero heads up or asking the right people. They don’t care about their people. They also don't get how stuff actually works, so they mess up big decisions. And guess who feels it? Our poor customers when you close all the branches. 

They splash out millions on these big, useless internal roadshows, preaching about putting customers first. How about actually using the money to actually improve things? The problem isn’t us not caring about customers—it's the executives making all the wrong calls.

Generous Benefits Package: Comprehensive healthcare, wellness programs, and annual bonuses are well above industry standards.
cons:
High Workload During Peak Times: During project launches, the workload can become intense, requiring long hours, which can be stressful.
Limited Career Advancement Opportunities: Although the company provides solid training and development, there are limited opportunities for vertical growth, especially in senior positions.
Slow Decision-Making: Due to the emphasis on collaboration, decision-making can sometimes be slow, with many layers of approval needed.
Outdated Office Infrastructure: While the company is tech-forward, some physical office spaces and equipment are outdated, impacting comfort and efficiency in the workplace.
Frequent Shifts in Strategy: There are occasional abrupt shifts in company goals, which can lead to confusion or disruption in ongoing projects.

summary: An Analytical Odyssey at HSBC: Navigating the Peaks and Valleys
advice: Working as an analyst at HSBC is a dynamic experience that comes with its share of challenges and rewards. The exposure to global finance, cutting-edge tools, and a commitment to professional development make it an excellent choice for those seeking a stimulating career. However, navigating through bureaucratic hurdles and facing stiff competition require resilience and adaptability. If you're up for the challenge, the analytical journey at HSBC can be a fulfilling one.
pros:
Cutting-edge Tools: The bank invests heavily in state-of-the-art analytical tools, making the job more efficient and intellectually stimulating. Access to these resources has allowed me to develop and sharpen my analytical skills, staying ahead in the ever-evolving world of finance.

Professional Development: HSBC places a strong emphasis on employee growth. The structured training programs and mentorship opportunities have been invaluable in honing my skills. The learning culture encourages continuous improvement and adaptability to the rapidly changing financial landscape.

Work-Life Balance: Contrary to the finance industry stereotype, HSBC fosters a relatively healthy work-life balance. The organization values employee well-being, offering flexibility and remote work options when needed.
cons:
Bureaucracy: Like any large organization, navigating through layers of bureaucracy can be cumbersome. Decision-making processes can be slow, hindering the agility needed in a rapidly changing financial environment.

Stiff Competition: Given HSBC's global reach, the competition among analysts can be intense. This can lead to high expectations and, at times, a stressful work environment. Meeting tight deadlines and delivering high-quality work consistently is a non-negotiable.

Communication Challenges: Due to the global nature of the business, coordinating with teams in different time zones can be challenging. This sometimes leads to miscommunication or delays in project timelines.

pros:
The pay and benefits at HSBC are really quite good, especially if your face fits and you get high ratings on your end of year review. Salary is excellent, there’s an annual ‘bonus’ (sorry - ‘variable pay’), and the pension scheme is non-contributory which is really unusual - you can add to it, but the company pays 10% of your salary at the lower end. Other benefits include ‘free’ (but taxable) BUPA healthcare if you want it.

Leeds (Stourton) has a good sized car park with some chargers for electric cars.
cons:
It’s quite honestly the most soul-destroying job I’ve ever had.

I work in a call centre - the building is shared with First Direct. We only currently have half the building - because everyone was working from home, half of the building was closed off. However, HSBC then decided everyone needed to be in the office for 60% of the time - except in Leeds, there aren’t enough desks to accommodate so they’ve kept it at 10% until they can reopen the rest of the building. Quite why we need to be in a physical office is anyone’s guess - the job is perfectly do-able from home, and in fact visiting the office is a pain; it’s noisy, there’s no difference to how we do the work, and it means our carbon footprint goes through the roof, not to mention the cost of fuel. Absolutely ridiculous. I’ve seen team managers on a ZOOM meeting with each other, all sat on separate desks IN THE SAME OFFICE, which is madness! WE DO NOT NEED TO BE IN THE OFFICE FOR THIS JOB. 

In common with most call centre jobs, the entry-level staff are treated as disposable assets. We are micro-managed to ridiculous levels, whilst being told that development is our responsibility. Managers listen to several calls a month and mark the quality - yes, ‘all your calls are recorded for training a monitoring purposes’. A separate audit team pick a call and do the same. Managers pick some ‘short’ calls to make sure you aren’t deliberately cutting-off customers - quite why you’d do this is anyone’s guess, if people _are_ doing this they might want to ask why, because it just assumes staff are lazy. Which isn’t the case. We’re given a monthly (yes, monthly!) meeting where we discuss our statistics - average handling time, hold time, after-call time, schedule adherence (did we take our breaks/lunches/training at the correct time etc). After-call is the biggest issue - woe betide you don’t go back into ‘ready’ immediately, because _obviously_ you’re slacking off. In fact, the entire management structure seems designed to find fault with everything, and try and catch you out. Indicates a lack of trust, which is usually a sign of bad management in my experience. Team managers seem to be employed for this purpose. They certainly don’t speak to customers. 

Additionally, adherence to procedures is seen as some sort of God. We use a system called ‘iKnow’ which rarely works properly, is incredibly complicated to follow, but not using it reduces the score if your call is picked up. If you can’t find what you want in the 3000 lines of Ariel-8 text, you have to ask a manager. Assuming they can be bothered getting back to you, it usually feels like you’ve put them out. Some managers are worse than others at displaying their ire that you’ve dared bother them. Being fair, some managers are great, others…not.

Any actual ‘tasking’ (ie anything that needs doing that doesn’t involve talking to customers) is usually offshored to somewhere in India. That means that those guys follow a checklist - if they need to check something, they send a message to the customer to call in so we can relay their message and take the 15minutes of abuse. Of course, the messages are often so vague as to be useless, so trying to work out what needs doing is ridiculously complex. Of course, we could do this in our department ourselves and we’d know exactly what is required, but the company would rather save a few quid to employ more auditors to pick fault with our work. We’re basically an answering service for India. Which is crap for us, and even worse for the customers. Probably explains why HSBC are so poor in the customer ratings - that, of course, is our fault as staff - we need extra customer service training. It’s not because the company is a bloated, complex mess. Ever wondered why First Direct (part of HSBC) do so well in the customer service ratings, even though the structure is basically the same? It’s because the company is more simplified, and there’s less to go wrong. It’s easier learning the job if your systems are simpler. HSBC might want to take note.

Oh - a special mention for holiday booking. Trying to get a holiday is like picking a fight with lions. The system used breaks up every day in sections. You’ll find some sections have 3 people allowed off, some 2, some 1. So, 6am until 8am may have 3 people allowed, 8 to 8:30am allows 1, 8:30 to 10am, 2 people. So if someone books the day off, it means that the next person can’t, because the half-hour from 8 to 8:30 is now booked up, and you have to practically beg someone for the time off. It’s like this for the whole year. The holiday booking is on a 12 month rolling system - the holiday planner for Feb 2025 is opened in Feb 24, March 25 in March 24 and so on. Means if you like the same time off every year, you often have to log in whilst on holiday to make sure you get in early when they open the next year planner - which is unreasonable. Not that anyone cares, of course - holidays don’t come on the list of ‘important things’. So it’ll never change.

In other words, the entire company is a mess which the lower-grade staff get the brunt of. The higher grade staff don’t care - they’re too busy trying to get promoted, which leads to a culture of blaming everyone else and stepping on others to get on. It’s toxic, it’s nasty, and I wouldn’t recommend. Although it’s no worse than any other call centre I’ve worked in, to be fair - call centre work is generally awful, and I have no idea why it has to be so bad. Probably because company directors have never actually done it. We spend a lot of time talking about people’s mental health, without addressing the causes of it in the first place - perhaps if the culture was better, the mental health of the staff would also improve, eh?

summary: Decent place to work. HEAVILY depends on the management. Can be EXTREMELY toxic (like Wimbledon)
advice: For goodness sake get better at your job you two network managers. Look at your neighbouring management and how happy their colleagues are. Stop pushing sales on the colleagues and making it all about the number. At the end of the day it is a customer service role and not car sales role. Happier colleagues stays with you for longer, saving you the time and hassle to recruit new people and train to be on the floor by themselves (which takes about 5 months very least). Be genuinely there for your colleagues, do not sit at the back and enjoy your coffee whilst laughing with your fellow managers and being on zoom calls. Do not talk about you know what is happening in the front floor if you are behind close doors having a chit chat and your coffee. Please learn how to talk to your colleagues. A very common MBA or a basic MA degree does not magically give you managerial skills, so please have some shame and respect for yourself, and act like a fully grown adult. There is no fixing the damage you’ve done with your fellow colleagues and your image you have portrayed at other branches. But at least it will fix something in the future. Also nobody cares about you doing 7 accounts on a Saturday. As grown adults we do not have time to give you a golden star for something you did 7 years ago.
pros: Decent benefits (Healthcare plan, pension matching, additional benefits like dental cover etc can be purchased) Colleagues were great at where I worked (Wimbledon). Very closely knitted, and had each other’s back. Good starting salary for a role that does not require any qualification. Also has an end of year review for salary appraisals and bonuses. If you are lucky enough, you can around to different interesting departments within HSBC.
cons: Absolute mockery of a management. The managers at my branch ( Wimbledon) were very incompetent, didn’t back the colleagues up and were pushing things down on the colleagues. They cut down the breaks from 1 hour to 30 minutes and eventually to 20 minutes. Whereas the other surrounding branches were getting their usual hour long breaks. We were also often forced to take 15 minutes or even 10 minute breaks because it is busy. The management promises to give back the hours or pay you for it, but the intentionally don’t keep their words. They are quite aware it would be swept under the carpet. Management makes the place a toxic work environment. Especially picking on colleagues for small errors, but never genuinely appraises them when they solve a complicated issue. No sufficient training for new colleagues. You get a training for 2 months, where 80% of the things are completely useless, and the rest 10% is some practical. You are thrown out to the front, and expect to perform miracles. Also you will be CONSTANTLY taking stick from the customer for the bank’s faults, errors and poor decisions. They take it out on the front staffs, and the management does jackstick about it.

advice: Do your job. Give people the right privileges to do their job, show appreciation, give a pay raise once in a blue moon at least. Keep a close look on your network managers, they often are the main reason people resign.

They will be rude and simply won’t do their job. So you’ll leave just like everyone else had before you.

pros:
Hand on heart, decent company culture with most of the senior managers truly passionate about diversity and inclusion. The UK retail bank is making great strides to become a financially inclusive brand that cares about the vulnerable in society. 
The company embraces flexible working, should you in a head office role, part-time, condensed hours, job share, flexible start/finish time, sabbatical, and the number of days in office are all open for discussion with your line manager.

From personal experience, there are plenty of line managers that are passionate about your development and really care about your wellbeing. You may call this luck, but remember, recruitment is a two-way thing. Try to learn about the job, team, and department beforehand, and my humble advice is to choose a good team and/or line manager over fancy titles.
cons:
How Simple Becomes Complicated is a well known phrase in HSBC. 
The executives have spent years trying to streamline and simplify, but the truth is: multiple layers of governance meetings are taking over everyone's time, and teams' responsibilities still overlay each other. 
With the recent job cuts, most departments are operating under bare skeleton. A lot of fire fighting on the ground every day.

This organisation rewards tenure over talent. Unless you started on a graduate scheme, you may usually find colleagues below your grade who has been with the Bank for 20/30 years earn more than you do. This obviously will discourage young talents to stay with the Bank and look for opportunities elsewhere.

summary: Good to start career, hard to make impact at scale
pros:
- Help you to discover area of interest. I didn’t know what I wanted to do straight after graduation, so I went for a retail banking graduate scheme at HSBC UK, I was lucky to get some good rotations and then decided to switch to data 
- Good work life balance - people are nice and chill, very rarely do an entry level grad (at least for teams I worked with) need to work over time, data team can sometimes be busier, but still very chill compare to other companies
- can work on big projects with strategic importance
- can get involved in very hybrid projects in certain teams, good to get data skills, i.e. you could be a full-stack data person, from initial analysis with visualisation to sketching out machine learning solution and productionising it to make real customer impact then monitoring the metrics throughout the product lifecycle/ upgrading through different iterations
cons:
- Hard to align incentives of different teams. Teams are very specialised, and one project typically include many internal/ 3rd party vendors, and they all have different priorities. So one project can hardly progress according to its planned timeline
- Broken data pipeline because systems are in migration all the time, which increases dependency on other teams and you return to problems in above point
- Unclear career ladder. My department only has junior and senior level and the gap between these two levels are big and hard to define + project delivery is very slow, there seems no decently quick track to progress to higher position
- Salary is not competitive for data roles (of course this depends on your team, this is just what I’m having now!)

summary: A great company with a lot on its plate right now
advice: HSBC's greatest strengths are its incredibly rich and diverse customer base, and equally the diverse range of people it employs around the world. The company could benefit from celebrating this more by putting its customers and people closer to the centre of its strategic objectives, which feel like they are architected to satisfy the analyst community and move the share price rather than establishing the long term purpose and sustainability of the company.
pros: "International" is perhaps the defining feature of HSBC. This means that many employees have opportunities to interact cross-culturally / cross-border, and being regularly exposed to such a diverse range of people, projects and challenges is very rewarding and interesting. HSBC has a collaborative culture where many opinions are sought and respected, and in my experience usually there is a pleasant working atmosphere. Senior management and people across the company mostly are serious about doing the right thing, and if ever HSBC can wire itself together to its full potential, there is so much opportunity for the company to be a real force for good.
cons: The banking industry is going through a pretty grim period of reshaping itself and HSBC is no exception. Recent high profile failures mean that implementing a complex regulatory and financial crime compliance agenda is critically important also recent disappointing financial performance is driving continual reorganisations. Both of these mean the company's rhythm can be focussed more on internal issues rather than looking outwards for opportunity and inspiration.

Negotiate well your entry salary, as it will never be raised until you are promoted, unlike other banks that provide yearly raises (which is the norm for global banking and global markets positions in tier 1 banks). There is very little encouragement to develop your career or move up in the bank - you have to fight your way up and this is nearly impossible if you are not a white British man.  The bonuses are shockingly low compared to what competitors are paying (in Capital Markets).  Very few people, particularly in senior management that you can look up to - most of them just seem to be bureaucrats.  In general, there are a lot people who don't do much work, but sit around from 9am-4pm and collect a salary (they were probably ambitious at some point until HSBC crushed it out of them). summary: Large organisation with a very flat management structure.  Hard to get promoted
advice:
The HSBC strategy of maintaining "positive jaws" (revenue must grow faster than costs every year) can sometimes cause people several layers below the CEO to make poor decisions.  In any company, the net profit should be allowed to fluctuate naturally due to market conditions.  Rigorous cost cutting comes at the expense of increased risk and reputational impact due to lower quality services.

In IT, the number of downtime events has been steadily increasing, due to the lack of knowledge in newer offshore resources meaning poorer quality work such as testing of changes, etc.  More care needs to be taken when exiting staff, to ensure that the overall cost to the company does not paradoxically increase to due to knowledge drain.  

Reputational impact can have a marked effect on profitability and thus getting rid of key knowledge workers from higher costs locations such as the UK is false economy.  The UK has some of the best IT staff in the world.  We have tried hiring top IT staff in many regions and the UK has the only location we have been able to consistently hire and keep the best minds.  Other companies are currently benefitting from HSBC's layoffs, taking their wealth of knowledge with them to help others build their competitive advantage.
pros:
The people!  It is a very diverse, multicultural and multinational environment.  You do most of your interaction via video and audio conferences (at least in IT) and you often have no idea which city some of the people on calls are in - could be India, US, Switzerland, China, you name it.  

You need to grow your network and get your name known for good positive work.  This will help you get good feedback and increase your performance review. 

People listen to anyone with good, strong and sound ideas.  Given the size of the organisation, not a lot of emphasis is placed on seniority, and you can quite happily engage with people several bands above and below you.  Just learn to treat everyone with dignity and respect, be brilliant at what you do, and you can make a name for yourself!
cons:
You are not likely to get promoted unless you are very junior.  The career bands are very protected and you have to be exceptional to get moved from GCB5 to 4, and a god to move from a GCB4 - 3!

Bonuses and pay remuneration of late have been quite suppressed, especially if you are a 40% tax payer already.  I had no pay rise for 3 years running with a "strong" rating.   If you are an average employee (70% of the population), you will get a "strong" rating.  "Strong" is just average - thats it.  No matter how clever you are or how hard you work, it is very hard to get recognised as "top", unless you are well connected and spend more time influencing than working.  I have found this quite unfair, as the people recognised are generally the loudest rather than the best.

With interest rates already going up a quarter point and set to rise again, the remuneration and bonus situation could change.

pros: Strong company culture, good work-life balance (dependent on team), friendly and inclusive culture, above average pay for a graduate scheme
cons:
I would like to add to the review left on 29 June 2020 for the Commercial Banking (CMB) Graduate Programme to reflect that the sentiment described was definitely not an isolated case - a lot of graduates had similar experiences.

Removing subjective judgments the CMB Graduate Scheme has been plagued by numerous problems - I would address two in this review. First, mismanagement. Across different cohorts graduates have been told at the very last minute of “sudden business changes” which required re-assignments from value-adding placements to basic call centre roles, and in at least two instances even a mandatory extension of at least six months to the 18-months programme graduates signed on to. What graduates signed on to was an 18-month national mobility situation, not what inevitability transpired as described. It was widely felt that there was complete disregard for any personal circumstances, where everyone was expected to accept this out-of-contract, unforeseen arrangement without protest (for any protest received admonishments for graduates being “ungrateful” and “entitled” and “having bad attitudes”), uproot themselves and resolve any logistical or financial issues at last-minute notice, with minimum to no support. 

Second, under-qualified graduate managers. While the above described could be explained as top-down instructions outside of the graduate team’s control being poorly executed by the graduate managers, the managers’ lack of CMB knowledge and lack of initiative to remedy that after years of being in the role was inexcusable. This was particularly problematic was because graduate placements were allocated by graduate managers, who screened placement applications. Graduates were told to write their applications in laymen terms, because if graduates included “technical banking terms”, the graduate managers would not be able to understand the application and would disregard those parts as irrelevant. This greatly affected the chances of graduates being placed in teams that best fit their skills and desired career paths. 

Numerous other issues could be raised with ample examples which would result in this review being unreadably long. I hope, however, that the detailed examples given in this review could give some context as to how the CMB graduate scheme was run. 

I could confirm here, however, that as stated in the 29 June 2020 review, favouritism and preferential treatments were existent, and that the high dropout rate of graduates particularly in the past year, as well as graduates taking time off due to the graduate programme compromising graduates’ mental health were true.

1) Boss would watch our tea breaks. When we come back from tea break he would always give us work. If contractor left early he blocks them at the lift and told them to go back to desk. 

2) Boss himself did no work and was on the phone with recruiters the whole time looking for work himself, at the same time trying to make sure we were all glued to our desks. We say him downstairs on the phone and even sitting at a cafe having tea with recruiters during office hours. 

3) Colleague bought a flat. Asked if he could buy some fx fwd at the time to hedge against Brexit. Boss ignored him. Brexit happened. His mortgage was in euros, he was earning pounds. Pounds crashed. 

4) Contractor found a new job. Out of politeness he told boss he was happy to stay for a few weeks to help with transition. Update the computer systems - the amount of time people waste on the internet not working or systems not working must equal millions of man hours across the organisation, and therefore millions of pounds.

One office will interpret a governance document completely differently from another and they will be so siloed that this will go on for years. Messages are not communicated effectively and the rumour mill is often weeks ahead of official announcements.

summary: good place to work with lots to improve

people are generally helpful and constructive to work with.

summary: Expect far too much for no reward. Constant complaints

cons: Unsociable hours, Bad management on every level. No scope for progression as they use secondments to back fill places and are making another round of redundancies which will put further stress on an already poor service due to lack of training.

summary: HSBC is a VERY average bank..
advice: Wake up and get rid of people who are simply not adding value. There are far to many layers within the organisation that are just not necessary. The global diversity team need to pull up their socks and actually do some work!
pros: Global company with overseas career opportunities. Great opportunities to work with colleagues around the globe. Generally a very easy and unchallenging place to work.
cons: Employees and line managers do not live by the firms values.  Productivity is slow! Very few role models. The culture (team/ department dependant) is generally pretty shocking.

summary: Not what it used to be
advice: Treating your staff like contractors means they will treat you like a temporary job.
pros: Good pension with 7% company match.  Big organisation which tends to prefer to promote internally.
cons: You are calibrated against your peers, so even if you meet all your targets if you aren't in the top whatever % then you aren't good.  It's a numbers game.  There are very few senior positions, so although they promote internally your chances of succeeding are small.  Training was second to none, but the new departments are not living up to this.

advice: Actually listen to those on the frontline.
pros: Benefits are honestly amazing. Sometimes makes it worth it all. Your direct line manager is amazing & will do everything in their power to support you. Great team dynamics .
cons: Literally everything else. Above your direct line manager, management don't care about you & let you know this on a daily basis. They make changes that almost never work which causes chaos. If they do respond to feedback, it's so slow & by the time it's implemented, it's out of date. Abuse off of customers is horrendous, from death threats, racial abuse & all sorts of other horrific things. You're expected to just get on with it. Upper management talk about mental health & how much they do, but it's empty words. They try to show how diverse & inclusive they are but its superficial & concerns aren't taken seriously. You're made to feel like it's your fault for interpreting it 'incorrectly'. Staff outside of BTB speak to BTB as if they are dirt beneath their shoes. You'r expected to do ABCDEF but given no support & very little guidance. They will not train you no matter how much you ask, always making up excuses as to why you cannot be trained on more lines. Keeping in mind, that if you are trained on all lines, you can move up a grade level. They have also recently gotten rid of this accreditation meaning you're stuck at the lowest level. Software & procedures are out of date, slow & difficult to use. You are not a bank worker so are expected to work bank holidays. Shifts are badly designed so at times you can be the only person from your management group on the phone. Referrals for customer questions are painful - half the time there is nobody available to answer so you're waiting 5 minutes +. Other half of the time, depending on who answers, you'll have a different solution. The job is mentally & emotionally draining.

pros:
Excellent work life balance.
Great career prospects but you need to be proactive in this space. Speak up and let your manger know you are ambitious and use the HSBC tool available internally.
cons:
Such a big company that at times it is hard to work out which team you need to go to. 
It can take time to onboard new staff and to get full system access...don’t be put off by the length of time if takes. Once on-boarded fully you should have a more positive experience at the bank.

summary: Conservative organisation searching for a role in the new digital world
advice:
-	Please be open-minded about people moving roles and give them a chance to change and open up.  Leaving people in the role for years makes people resentful and will lower their longterm performance.   
-	What does good look like when culling the 35k workforce has been done?  The organisation is still a federation of banks rather than a collective and the inefficiencies still remain where multiple countries have similar teams doing the same work.
pros:
-	Depending on where you are in the organisation it can be great to be able to move around if you are younger and have the qualifications.
 -	Can pay well if your role is in demand.
-	The painful process Noel Quinn (CEO) has embarked upon to shed 35 k staff is going to shake up the bank and its capabilities which is welcome unless you're living it internally the negative impact is that there is incredible pressure to cover roles which are no longer recruited and people in some areas they doing long hours with no end in sight.
-	Female managers see more chances of promotion than previously but there are still large enclaves of male-dominated non-white sexist pockets in different areas. ( btw I am male )
cons:
-	Managers can be particularly arrogant but may have multiple faces.
-	Hard to move roles at some stages of your career, seniors closed about some people if they have formed a negative view.
-	I saw lots of people who are in the older generation 'locked' into their role and unable or unwilling to put their hand up for change as the result could be negative.
-	Some senior managers manage to stay in role for years without developing themselves or being able to be developed.
-	It started to become more autocratic in management style choosing to command and control. This probably depends on which area you work in.
- The chain of command can be so vague that your manager doesn't understand what you do and what your skill set is and hence development can be challenging.
-	Achieving band 3 middle management is an achievement but every 5 years they have a clear-out and more band 3's are removed at every cull.
-	The middle market is dominated by HSBC and it beats other banks hands down, the market is more lucrative generally that S&P 500 which has razor-thin margins, the negative side is that RMs typically handle huge portfolios of 80+ clients and do not get to know their customers and can be worked intensively.

summary: Still far too many Ivory Towers
advice: Cut down on the management consultants, and trust in your own staff.  Many of the senior leadership are now ex-BGC or Bain or McKinsey and what works on a PPT often doesn't work in real life when you don't understand the people or the customer.    Walk the floors and get real with the open communication, "speak openly - but don't say anything that management doesn't want to hear" is not open communication.   If all you hear is good news, something is definitely wrong!  Get rid of the annual AOP process, it is holding you back!  The world has changed and Agile is a way of working, not something you feel after a yoga class.
pros: Still has a very international culture, and has huge opportunities if people are empowered to make the changes required. Decent culture although for all the talk about doing the right thing, much of this remains warm air in many circles.
cons: Not one bank but 3 separate banks, operating in 4 different regions. Huge legacy of antiquated systems, and little appetite to really approach this. Very heavy top management layers, with major ivory tower syndrome. Bad news or messaging stays a middle management level. Go against that at ones own risk! Zero HR department, or rather zero assistance from HR, who make up a large % of staff, but have outsourced 98% of tasks either to HRdirect website, or to Centre of Excellence in India. If Aliens were to abduct 90% of the UK/Global HR function, the business would continue without realising they were gone. I wont comment on what the Alien's would make of them, but fair to say they may leave with a relatively poor opinion of the work ethics on planet earth.

summary: Honest, fair and true of my experience
advice: With a character limit of this box I’m not sure I can fit all of my advice to management in it.
pros: #NAME?
cons:
The Swansea ‘contact-centre’ is one of the most unwelcoming and toxic work environments I’ve ever experienced. 

From the get-go you are treated as just a number by management and ‘colleagues’ around you. 9 other people started the same time as myself and within the first three months 6 had resigned largely due to job dissatisfaction. The training group I joined were all herded on the telephones as quickly as possibly with abject and minimal training (3 days out of the 20 days training was spent covering a topic which is not relevant to the role). 

The training provided was by a third-party company and not HSBC, therefore, information that was being provided in training was out-of-date and not in line with current policy and procedure.

Myself and others had first-hand experiences of harassment and bullying from selective colleagues and managers. One particular incident I remember is a ‘senior’ manager trying to make an example of me in front of the office floor of 15/20 people. I cannot give the specific example because it will probably identify who I am , and I’m confident the managers will have a good-laugh about how they tried to belittle me . This example is just one of many within the Swansea ‘call-centre’ of management being pedantic about trivial issues instead of managing staff properly and providing a high level of customer service. 

After this particular incident I lost all respect for management within the ‘call-centre’ and immediately started looking for alternative employment. 

Conflicting information from employee to employee! Because the organisation is so large, it’s hard to have consistent messages communicated. I found that i’d come in one morning and one senior is telling you one thing and another manager another, which in a customer service role can lead to very irate and annoyed customers if you’re not providing accurate information.

Finally, I found the job to be repetitive and soul- destroying as you deal with 40/50 calls a day, the large majority of these customers are already irate before you speak to them because they’ve been waiting in a queue for 40-50 minutes (on a good day). 

This job could be for some people but not for myself, the ‘call-centre’ environment has a low ‘ceiling’ when it comes to progression and pay, the mortgage department was littered with employees who had been in the job for 10-15 years and were still earning £17,500, for people with ambition I would say the ‘call-centre’ is not for you.

summary: Not Disability Confident. Head of HR, CEO Ian Stuart, Noel Quinn haven't replied back to letters, even 1 year later
pros: Variety of roles for starting career as graduate, then look at other companies for career growth.
cons:
Senior Team Management are not engaged with their staff, not interested in keeping you there long term, even if you have worked there over 10 years. 

Very Self-focused environment, rather than building a great team community in the workplace. 

Management team not available for support if you have a problem, they don't come back to you at all and are difficult to get hold of them, even though they tell you to give them positive feedback for their staff survey appraisal, tell you which boxes to tick for the questions that apply to them. 

Sadly not a place where females can thrive, very few opportunities in this decade, even development programmes as female management. 

Not flexible if you want to work part-time in management role as a woman, very rigid, old fashioned.

They are not transparent on salary, hide benefits from you, stop you from talking with other peers and women are not on the same pay as men for same grade. Other employees advertise more honestly and you know what you will be getting as its all on the job posting. 

Didn't look after staff at all over Covid, made lots of job cuts and didn't provide furlough at all, even though the Government made this specifically available for businesses to use and to help their employees, this in itself says a lot about this brand, when other smaller organisations such as NFU did not make any job cuts at all. In the media they ran adverts to say how they are helping over Covid, but behind doors reality is a different story. Not honest in the media that they didn't use Furlough and that they cut jobs. 

I would recommend candidates to invest in a brand which is more up to date with Modern times, as they will struggle to hold onto good staff (this isn't the place for millennials who are ambitious and for women who want to progress), has ethical practices in place in the workplace, transparent and cares about how it treats its staff.

summary: TIME TO ABANDON SHIP - A shadow of its former glory and sadly sinking fast behind the scenes
advice:
I don't write this review lightly - Management need to take stock and seriously review large portions of the bank.

1) Salaries - This is HSBC's number one issue.  If you pay peanuts, you'll get monkeys.  These are in desperate need of attention.  Mid and low management are clearly fed a line that 'salaries are reviewed by HR regularly and are market average' even though they are around half of what the average market is.  Even when shown evidence that this is not the case, no action is taken and results in a great deal of staff leaving because of it.  A good example of this was the department I worked in was paid just over half of what the market average is and resulted in less than a year over 3/4 of the department (consisting of around 40 staff) leaving because of salary along with style of management. 
2) Learn to listen - I mean really listen, not just say you are listening.  You have a pool of individuals ready and willing to provide constructive feedback which could really help improve the business but you refuse to listen to them.
3) Stop promoting people simply because of their gender - HSBC sometime ago were singled out for not having enough women in their senior management and seem to have gone overboard, now being very openly discriminating against promoting male employees.  Gender equality should be exactly that, equal.  Openly promoting individuals purely based on their chromosomes.  
4) Address the recruitment preference culture - HSBC's internal recruitment process is very much a case of WHO you know rather than WHAT you know.
For example, HSBC have a policy that for every job placement advertised that a minimum of 2 individuals are interviewed for it.  This clearly doesn't always happen as I've seen instances where for 2 job placements advertised only 2 people were interviewed in a morning and immediately after they had finished the second interview, it was announced to the wider team.  

In conclusion, a very disappointing bank to work for and I can't see it surviving this way in the long run.  Senior management seem more interested in keeping the shareholders happy and how much of a profit they can make rather than paying staff what they deserve to be paid which in turn is breeding a harmful culture filled with morally corrupt individuals.
pros:

Low salaries also regrettably prevent most employees from taking full benefit of the benefit schemes on offer. Bonuses are increasingly being stripped down to nothing even for those who perform well at their jobs. 
2) Culture of micromanagement - I could go on about this for hours but I have even seen first hand management follow employees to the toilet and stand by the sinks waiting for them to finish only to walk them back to their desk.
3) A culture of covering up issues - This by no means reflects the entirety of HSBC.  I have friends who are very happy in the departments they work in however there is increasingly a culture of mid and senior management covering issues up, including but not limited to, thieving (i.e. employees being caught stealing money from colleagues), discrimination (i.e. racial and sexual), sexual harassment (i.e. mid management groping intimate parts of junior colleagues without their permission), workplace misconduct (i.e. mid management coming in to work virtually every day stinking of alcohol, shooting off for a boozy lunch and never returning).  Reporting these issues to HR very rarely led to any action being taken. 
4) Overall poor working environment - You are contracted 09:00-17:00 in most jobs with a 1 hour lunch break.  With that said, in most jobs you are expected at your desk before at least 08:45 with your computer started up, if you are seen packing up even as early as 17:05 you are judged for it and there is no paid overtime.

jobTitle: John Lewis Financial Services Customer Service
summary: I would never recommend working here.
advice:
- Pay your staff's wages 
- Ensure your managers actually know employment law before they try to breach it

pros: Allegedly there's career progression opportunities after 12 months but I didn't see any evidence of this.
cons:
They're refusing to pay my wages. I started work there at the beginning of December, they attempted to prevent me from receiving notice pay when I handed my notice in. 

I was offered a job, given a start date and time and told to await paperwork, I made financial decisions based on this, then was told 3 weeks later that I'm being put into a "Talent pool" and can't start on my offered day as they'd hired too many people for the position and my name had randomly picked to be pushed back until the next intake. Months later I recieved another offer, with paperwork and advised I needed to go through vetting. 

An entire month of 0 communication later, a 3rd party vetting company in London then demanded I signed a document giving them the right to demand ANY information they later request as well as ring up any of my previous employers and ask them ANYTHING, even non-emplpoyment related, which goes well outside the scope of what is reasonable. All of this, including seriously sensitive and private information I would never give to an employer, or anyone, was also expected to be sent to this stranger in London, who additionally,  I had no agreement under the GDPR to share or store any of this with, it would be going through personal email, completely unsecured. Interesting how HSBC allows this but wouldn't even allow us to login to our work emails from home because of customer's data protection.

My "case" was then allegedly referred to HSBC's legal department who advised the information I'd already provided was sufficient and I didn't need to communicate further with this 3rd party to get my start date and begin.

On breaks and lunches I heard nothing but trained staff talking about how miserable it was, they couldn't wait to leave, they were all applying elsewhere and it was awful.

I'd also had some disgusting comments made about my disability by other staff members.

We were also told about all this support we'd receive and that we were going to be doing 1-2-1s with a manager every month to keep track of our wellbeing. My "class" completed the first one, I wrote about all of the above (paraphrased) and a manager whipped around the class, signed them all off and didn't bother to read them.

My dream job then offered me a position, so I handed my notice in and said I want to work (It would be a week on the phones so I'd be taking thousands of pounds of payments towards credit cards, at least 10 times daily what I'd be earning in a month working there) and I was told that I wasn't allowed to work my notice, wouldn't be getting paid notice pay, and that I needed to he escorted out of the building either then or at the end of the day. The two trainers we had, one of whom was communicating all of this, were lovely and incredibly knowledgable, and was just communicating what a manager, who wouldn't even look me in the eye, had told her.

Now, weeks later, I haven't been paid, despite my ex-colleagues being paid on Saturday and contractually needing to be paid on Monday, because out of 1 of the 3 times I had to submit my bank details clearly wasn't enough for them to input it correctly. That's even if the payslip ive been sent, without a P45 which has been requested numerous times as well as my actual wage, is accurate and they have attempted to pay this money, which I'm starting to doubt is really the case. 

Knowing what I know about various goings on in this bank, I would never work for them again and never bank with them. Just as a bonus, John Lewis Financial Sercives, which was the department I worked for, were all very vocal about other department stores going under but not once mentioned how John Lewis were struggling. (Not commercially sensitive as it was never bought up in the course of the employment by any means and was later discovered by myself on a Telegraph Article from October 26th 2019)

As a bonus, one of my classmates persistently bragged about sharing a car with his dad and accruing numerous penalty points, PCNs and had multiple car crashes but kept and keeps giving his dad's information out to his record is clean. These are the kind of people working there who've passed vetting and openly discuss this on the floor.

I've been extremely polite, patient and reasonable with the completely innocent HR staff who I've been communicating with over the unlawful deduction of wages and failure to pay the national minimum wage, but they've in fact advised that not only are my bank details now correct and payroll were made aware first thing Monday morning of the situation, that several people have been directly emailed to rectify the situation  it's been logged 3 times as urgent and escalated tonthebhighest point it can be escalated, and not one of them have responded or have done anything.

summary: I'd rather chew my foot off than go back there
advice:
Show your staff respect (you may need to research what that actually means).
Introduce 360 degree feedback, and act on it.  Yes there'll be cost, but you get far more out of staff  who are engaged, empowered and motivated, than staff who are fearful, resentful and brow-beaten.
pros:
Strong track record, one of the few financial institutions that weathered recent storms relatively unscathed
It's a large organisation and there are lots of opportunities: some staff seem to do very well in terms of promotions / responsiblities etc
They're generally well-organised
"My choice" reward package gives you some good choices of non-cash benefits as part of your remuneration package e.g. BUPA healthcare for you & your family.
Good training programmes.
Most colleagues are decent people, some departments have a good social life.
cons:
Wages are deliberately set at 10% below the market median.
Frequent restructuring and re-orientation of goals etc means there is a lack of continuity - 100s of man hours invested in projects & initiatives, then one day your boss says "we're not doing that anymore".  Inefficient and frustrating.
Excessive red tape and a "can't do" attitude amongst middle management.  
A big vote up here for the brainwashing.  Every day you're told HSBC is "The Best Place to Work" - this slogan is plastered across foyers in letters 6 foot high.  And for years I believed it... TBH I started to believe there must be something wrong with me, always missed out on promotions, getting poor reviews, very undervalued.  Back at School, Uni and everywhere else I've worked I was always a high achiever, yet at HSBC I always felt like a ne'er do well.  Why?  Because line managers generally don't like people with ideas and initiative, they want Stepford Wives.  
[BTW, HSBC is not "The Best Place to Work".  Back in the days when *all* staff completed the staff survey, we used to score 55%-60% staff satisfaction.  There are 100's of companies in the country with staff satisfaction ratings >90%.]
Bullying is rife.  Too many managers throwing their weight around.  Over 12 years I had 9 different line managers, I made complaints against 3.  Not only were my complaints not investigated, HR told me I would be placed on a disciplinary for gross misconduct if I didn't retract a formal grievance. In case you're thinking I'm the over-sensitive whiny type, one complaint was i.r.o. a physical assault, witnessed by numerous colleagues.  Nothing was done about it, no-one would back me up.  People didn't want to "get involved".
My opinion is that HSBC's anti-bullying policy is there for show, like a lot of their other policies.  e.g. I also suffered RSI whilst working at HSBC, they took 3 months to undertake a workstation assessment and refused to provide me with an ergonomic mouse - I had to buy my own.  
Morale is low, so many staff I've seen in tears, even threatening suicide because they hate their jobs so much.
Poor communication & secrecy at every level of management.  e.g. Time and time again staff have found out from BBC news that HSBC is making 1000 UK staff redundant, but there is zero internal communication about it.  Staff are left to worry and speculate, whispering in corners.
Regarding IT systems - yes a lot are fairly stone-age.  HSBC overall tend to "play it safe", which is one of the reasons they didn't fall into the money market sinkhole back in 2007/2008, but it also means they choose to avoid being at "the leading edge" of anything, because the leading edge is often the bleeding edge.
Also ofc new things cost money: if you've not worked for a financial institution, please understand that everything is about money.  And it seems nothing else matters.

summary: Terrible employer with branches the worst
advice: Your staff are unhappy, overworked and stressed, and you take them for granted despite their being driven, intelligent and talented.  Something is drastically wrong and it is your cost cutting strategy. Constant staffing cuts leading to increasingly poor service levels which branch staff are left to apologise for - shocking when historically service has been great
Constant motivational speaking guff to cover up for obvious problems rather than actually trying to fix any of them
You are expected to devote your life to HSBC, be relentlessly positive and treat every scrap from the table you are given as manna from heaven while accepting ever more punitive conditions
You're told that there are no sales targets and you won't be expected to push products, but then you are, and because it's at a local level it never gets noticed

pros:

They prioritise recruiting internally; once you're in, you can "sidestep" in to other jobs they have within the company fairly easily, for example from the mortgages department over to customer services. There are seniors that put their heads down and work hard, but are completely overlooked when manager positions open up.

advice: Your performance framework discriminates against PRMs who work in smaller branches, as does the lack of PRO support.  This places huge additional burdens on those PRMs in terms of generating appointments and banking needs.  Morale has collapsed and in my region, 90% of PRMs who were active when I joined have resigned.  The robotic slave like addiction to weekly appointment targets is incredibly destructive.   I refused to make up appointments in my diary (unlike my fellow PRMs) and instead focused on quality appointments.  As a result, my monthly revenue targets were top quartile, while appointments per week were bottom quartile.  One target does not influence the other.  PRMs should be targeted on overall profitability and not new credit cards or mortgages, especially when given small regional branches.  However, the middle management are too scared to challenge the senior management, and the senior management refuse to accept responsibility for this debacle.  Net effect.  Nothing changes.  People resign.  Customer satisfaction with the bank collapses and the bank waste millions recruiting new PRMs to replace those who have resigned without tackling the underlying reasons.   No doubt the bank will boost salaries for those that are left, but you are also destroying the fabric of your business relying on outdated management techniques that are far to generalised  and simplistic.

summary: Oh dear.....what a car crash company
advice: If there is one thing I would say to the CEO; you need to look at Junior Management within GBM sector as this is where your high costs are yet they are covering up losses and maintaining poor standards.  Doing something purely for the sake of doing something, is a common theme unfortunately " because that's how it's always been done".  'Thinking' is not allowed.   Sad to say, but I wouldn't be surprised to hear of another multi-million dollar regulatory fine happening in future; a case of when not if.
pros:
Prestigious name (just about) - HSBC still remains one of the world's biggest and oldest financial institutions.

Pension - One of the strongest in the financial services sector.  'Lifer's in Back Office accrue huge pensions!

Salary - HSBC pays above market rate for the level of work performed.   A lot of roles in Head Office include back office processing by individuals on high salaries (and costly pension programs).
cons:
Chaotic - HSBC is still incredibly disjointed, with basic systems not working, PC's crashing and not even having functioning lifts and building passes (this was none other than Head Office!)

Culture - HSBC is still in the dark ages with how it operates.  There is a clear divide between Junior Management (G4) and those beneath within departments.  There are clear themes of nepotism which breeds only a shielded culture and no openness or willingness to admit fault.  

Competencies - Unfortunately, a lot of staff are not equipped to work within the sector.  Hires are usually based upon whom managers personally like as opposed to just capability based therefore staff are generally within their 40's as an average and not exactly dynamic & challenging.  This unfortunately maintains the same poor standard and people do not think, they just do.

Progression - forget about it.  Speak to any former employee and they will repeat that there is a glass ceiling; Junior/Middle Management look after their own and that's it therefore sadly progression just does not happen.  Performance reviews are designed to talk you down for fear of creating more work in having to recruit new people therefore it's no surprise to see back office analysts at the age of 39!

summary: If you can think independently and are intelligent don't work here - you need to be a Stepford Wife.
advice:
Listen! Listen! Listen!   And don't assume you know better.
Look after the people and the work will look after itself.
Customers should occupy the positions of first, second, third, fourth and fifth in priorities followed by staff on the coal face, not being relegated somewhere down the list after managers status, managers egos, and managers bonus payments.
Scrap the current review process - it simply does not work and you are hacking off great staff who come in and just get on with their job, and do it very well, whereas less capable staff who know how to play the game and spend too much time feathering their own nest, appear to be valued more highly...... great in theory, but too open to abuse and misuse.  Too easy to use as a weapon if ANY manager does to like you (peer group ranking..... Ha!! What a farce) Supporting evidence too woolly and inconsistent. Comes down to how much you can massage the ego of your line manager and suck up to the other managers. Appeal process too complicated and too daunting to the point where it is tantamount to having to prove beyond any shadow of doubt that you are not a liar (this is very insulting). The whole process is like trying to pull a Sherman Tank sideways.
Stop abuse of authority - "I must be right because I am this grade.  What can you possibly Know?". JFDI whether you like it or not.  Whether it is honest or not.
Start Adult:Adult culture and single status culture instead of parent:child (i have four grown up children - one of which is older than my former line manager) 
Start a compulsory 360 degree feedback process that has teeth.
Stop suppressing entrepreneurial skills - this used to make HSBC great..... Not any more.
For Goodness Sakes do something about salaries.... And don't continue to cut the pay of longer serving staff through the back door of pensions. My take home pay was significantly more 5 Years ago than when i left (and that's without factoring in inflation).
I am lucky in that I do not have to work for you any more and I count my blessings every day (i took a significant pay cut to get away from you) But for the sake of the colleagues I left behind, LISTEN!
pros:
HSBC is great for customer service.
HSBC has a fantastic reputation
Senior Management are fantastic at steering HSBC to profitability and stability, and appear to have a 6th sense in accurately predicting ahead.
You will be very well trained and develop new skills
The majority of staff are very nice and helpful as people
cons:
HSBC are experts in brainwashing staff into believing that HSBC is the centre of the universe and their way is the right way. Life does not exist outside of the Bank. They are experts in spin doctoring.
Very poor wages and poor promotional opportunities above a certain level
Lack transparency in review process - its a popularity contest and is dependant upon how best you can suck up to your manager
Lack of unbiased validation of personal achievements for performance reviews- this means that some individuals can massage the statistical evidence of their achievements to make it appear they are doing a better job than they are. Specific examples provided to the bank by me were brushed under the carpet and disregarded. 
Misuse of authority - a great deal of bullying - instead of embracing the skills of individuals, managers with inferior skills will suppress the individual to avoid being exposed themselves. The bank officially takes bullying seriously but seems incapable of preventin it.
Very much a parent:child culture - managers condescendingly dictate to how you should feel, what your personal values should be. You need to leave "you" at the door and act as the person they want you to be in this unnatural, contrived environment.
Far, far too much politics with managers putting their own egos before what is beneficial to the company or the customer. This must be very expensive for the bank with wasted effort, wasted time in meetings and wasted use of resource.
The bank stopped undertaking general staff surveys years ago...... But now select a sample of individuals....... Read between the lines.
Don't believe that your working week is 35 hours. "To show your conviction and commitment..." expect to work somewhere between 45 and 50+ hours per week (for no extra pay) travelling in your own time even if this takes 3 or 4 hours on the train to attend meetings or site visits, and setting off at stupid-o-clock in the morning..... And does the bank value this? Read between the lines.
Most companies will say that their staff are their most valuable asset. HSBC does not appear to subscribe to this.  Their policy appears to be one where they will make life difficult and intolerable for longer serving staff so they leave and can be replaced by new (cheaper) staff. They do not value knowledge, experience, skills, innovation.  Don't get me wrong at interview they will test all of these, but they will knock any individuality out of you in the first 6 months.  They must have unreserved subservience. "If you don't like the way we do things..... hard cheese.... Leave!" this is their attitude. 
The bank is unreceptive to feedback and arrogantly "knows better".
I gave 3/4 of my working life to HSBC and feel stupid in that I have just realised how little they value you and I am horrified that they blatently do not even care that they do not value you. Moreover, many people you speak to seem to know someone who has had similar experiences with the bank and had to leave. The bank appears to have no humanity at all.

advice:
HBCS has been spending so much money on internal courses and propaganda to staff members on how important it is to do the right thing. You spend so much money on that, but then you don't actually do an audit and go to your first line of defense to analyse how that message is being implemented by people you are paying a lot of money to and if they’re adhering to it. People who you are paying a lot of money to ensure they are doing their jobs right. 

You should treat the people you employ right. We are customers too. We have families and friends and lives outside work. Surely, you'd want for your employees to recommend the institution they work for to their friends and family? People are leaving and spreading the word around in the industry (I am hoping you are connected to reality and understand that everyone knows everyone or knows someone who knows someone in the industry) and word of mouth right now within the industry is not positive. 
To be honest, it makes me sad. HSBC has the potential to be a great Bank! Unfortunately, they insist on hiring the same type of people over and over again and expect different results. cons:

This is absolutely great if there were roughly equal amount of male and female candidates in the market. Unfortunately when it comes to the IT department, there is simply more males than females in the job market hence making the hiring process extremely tedious as you need to wait till a female candidate to come up even if you found a perfectly fine male candidate. 

Making it worse, even if the hiring team manages to interview the same amount of males and females but eventually decides to make an offer to the male candidate, the upper management could cancel such an offer if the male candidate is not performing significantly better than the female candidates. 

As a result, the lower management would prefer to interview females even if their technical skills are just so-so and avoid males completely to be rid of the hassle of having to explain to the upper management.

summary: A Time wasting, Costly, and Disorganized Recruitment Experience
pros: The recruitment process completely shattered the positive expectations I had about HSBC.
cons:
I had an extremely frustrating experience with the HSBC recruiting process at the Havelock Mireka Tower branch. After completing the interview and assessment, they spent nearly 3 months just to conduct document verification. Despite frequently asking about my salary expectations, they kept postponing the conversation, saying it would be discussed after the verification. 

They requested an overwhelming number of documents, including a Gramasevaka certificate, a 5 year police report, employment certificates, house agreements, bank statements to prove previous salaries, landlord letters, landlord id copies, letter from parents etc. I even had to pay Rs. 15,000 just to translate my house agreement! After all that effort, they came back with a ridiculously low salary offer, claiming it was the maximum they could offer for the role.

What’s the point of collecting all these documents if they weren’t even going to meet my salary expectations? The process was a complete waste of time, energy, and money. This level of disorganization and lack of transparency makes me wonder how they treat employees if they handle candidates with such disregard.

1. **Global Presence**: HSBC operates in over 60 countries, providing extensive international exposure and opportunities for career growth and mobility across different regions.

2. **Diverse Workforce**: With a presence in multiple countries, HSBC promotes a diverse and inclusive work environment, encouraging a broad range of perspectives and cultural experiences.

3. **Strong Brand Reputation**: HSBC is recognized globally as a reputable and reliable financial institution, which can enhance professional credibility and provide stability.

4. **Career Development Opportunities**: HSBC invests in its employees' professional growth through training programs, mentorship opportunities, and clear career progression paths.

5. **Innovation Focus**: HSBC is committed to digital transformation and innovation, offering employees the chance to work on cutting-edge financial technology projects and initiatives.

6. **Comprehensive Benefits**: The company offers a wide range of benefits, including competitive salaries, bonuses, health and wellness programs, and retirement plans.

7. **Corporate Social Responsibility**: HSBC is involved in various sustainability and community development initiatives, allowing employees to contribute to meaningful causes while working for the company.

8. **Stability and Resilience**: As a well-established institution with a long history, HSBC has a strong foundation and resilience in the financial industry, offering employees a sense of job security.

These pros make HSBC an attractive employer for professionals seeking growth, international exposure, and a stable, reputable work environment.
cons:
While HSBC has many strengths, there are some potential drawbacks to consider:

1. **Large Bureaucracy**: As a massive global organization, HSBC can have complex and rigid structures, leading to slower decision-making processes and less flexibility.

2. **Pressure and High Expectations**: Working for a leading global bank can come with significant pressure to meet high performance standards, which can lead to a demanding work environment.

3. **Frequent Restructuring**: HSBC has undergone several restructuring efforts in recent years, leading to uncertainty and changes in job roles or redundancy for some employees.

4. **Regulatory Scrutiny**: Being a large, international bank, HSBC is often under intense regulatory scrutiny, which can result in a heavily compliance-driven environment that may feel restrictive.

5. **Work-Life Balance Challenges**: Due to its global operations, employees may face long hours or the need to accommodate different time zones, which can impact work-life balance.

6. **Cultural Differences**: The diverse and global nature of HSBC’s operations can sometimes lead to challenges in navigating different work cultures and communication styles across regions.

7. **Less Agility**: Compared to smaller, more nimble financial institutions or fintech companies, HSBC might be slower to adopt new technologies or innovate quickly due to its size and regulatory obligations.

8. **Customer Complaints and Reputational Issues**: HSBC has faced some high-profile scandals and customer complaints over the years, which might affect employee morale or the public perception of the company.

These factors should be considered by those looking at HSBC as a potential employer, especially if they value agility, a strong work-life balance, or a smaller company culture.

The operation guidelines undergo weekly updates, aiming to create an appearance of thorough regulation. While the intention behind meticulous record-keeping systems is commendable, the practicality is often lost amidst overwhelming workload demands. Employees find it challenging to complete their daily tasks and maintain meticulous system recordings, even within extended hours.

Compounding this issue is the hierarchical structure that places frontline bankers at the lowest tier, leaving them vulnerable to arbitrary deductions in performance points by back-office personnel. This lack of autonomy and inability to defend oneself against such deductions creates a sense of unfairness and frustration among employees.

Furthermore, the system's evaluation criteria seem to disproportionately penalize individuals for subjective reasons, such as perceived lack of respect, leading to additional deductions and potential loss of bonuses.

To foster a healthier work environment, it's essential to strike a balance between regulatory requirements and practicality. This can involve revisiting and refining operational procedures to streamline processes and reduce unnecessary burdens on frontline staff. Additionally, establishing transparent and equitable mechanisms for performance evaluation and feedback is crucial for boosting morale and fostering a culture of mutual respect and understanding

pros: A bank teller plays a crucial role in providing customer service and performing various financial transactions within a bank or credit union. Here's a summary of the key responsibilities and duties typically associated with a bank teller job: 1. Customer Service: Bank tellers are the front-line representatives of the bank and are responsible for delivering excellent customer service. They greet customers, address inquiries, and assist with account-related questions. 2. Cash Handling: Tellers process various financial transactions, including cash deposits, withdrawals, and check cashing. They must accurately count and verify currency and checks to ensure transactions are error-free. 3. Account Maintenance: Teller duties often include updating customer account information, such as address changes, and processing account transfers or closures as requested by customers. 4. Sales and Referrals: Bank tellers may identify opportunities to cross-sell or promote the bank's products and services, such as savings accounts, certificates of deposit, loans, and credit cards. They may refer customers to appropriate bank specialists for more complex financial needs. 5. Security Measures: Tellers are responsible for adhering to strict security protocols to prevent fraud and maintain the security of the bank. This includes verifying customer identities and following established security procedures. 6. Record-Keeping: Tellers maintain accurate records of all transactions, reconcile their cash drawers at the end of each day, and report any discrepancies. 7. Compliance: Bank tellers must adhere to federal and state banking regulations and policies to ensure compliance and protect the bank's interests. 8. Technology Usage: They use computer systems and specialized software to process transactions, access customer account information, and perform various banking operations. 9. Communication: Effective communication skills are essential for bank tellers to explain banking policies and procedures to customers and resolve any issues or discrepancies. 10. Teamwork: Tellers often work as part of a larger banking team, collaborating with colleagues, supervisors, and other departments to provide comprehensive banking services. 11. Multitasking: This role requires the ability to handle multiple tasks simultaneously, such as serving customers in person or over the phone while processing transactions accurately. 12. Professional Appearance: Bank tellers are expected to maintain a professional appearance and demeanor to represent the bank in a positive and trustworthy manner. Overall, a bank teller's job is to ensure the efficient and accurate handling of financial transactions while providing excellent customer service and adhering to security and compliance measures.

summary: What is it like to work at HSBC?
pros: 1. Size - HSBC stands tall in one of the top 10 banks of the world (by their total assets), which you could take pride in. 2. Salary - One must know that foreign banks are one of the best pay masters amongst all the industries. They usually pay at the higher side in comparison to most of the other companies. HSBC is no different. 3. Appraisals - They have excellent pay-outs at the time of appraisals, which is mostly in double digits (>10%). 4. Bonus - Again, the foreign banks have the best pay-outs in terms of performance bonus. At HTI this is usually 1 to 2 times of monthly salary and paid in the month of March yearly. 5. Work-life balance - Superb in most of the cases. Work from Home (WFH) - As every employee is issued a laptop, WFH is a trend here. Taking WFH once or twice in a month is absolutely normal here. 6. Holidays - One is entitled to 30 days of privileged leaves in a year, on top of 4 days of public holidays. In total, 34 leaves. There are sick leaves too which one could avail upto 10 days in a year. There is no other leave alloted on festive occasions like Holi, Eid, Diwali, X'mas, etc. However, one is free to take leaves on those occasions from their leaves balance. Also, out of those 30 privileged leaves one has to take 10 days (equivalent to 2 weeks) of mandatory vacation in one stretch which is called core leave at HSBC. One could take the core leave anytime of the year. The best part is at HSBC everyone is bound to consume 30 privileged leaves in a year as there is no mechanism to carry-forward the remaining leaves to the next financial year. So one gets to be away from work for quite a good amount of time, unlike many other organizations.
cons: 1. Lately, the promotions have become slow at HTI. There is no certain timeline for a person to get promoted. One could take 3–5 years (or even more) to get promoted, wherein a lot depends on manager and the kind of team one is into. 2. As HTI has no external clients and it works only for the HSBC group, there are only few on-shore opportunities, unlike many IT companies.

advice: Implement mandatory 360 feedback across the bank soonest possible which should help flush out bad management and hiring practices in the near term. Review and revamp compensation framework by balancing the benefits with salary better. Staff can't monetize the benefits to tackle inflationary daily expenses and if you pay peanuts, you get monkeys.
pros: Benefits are the best and most generous in HK; Co-workers are very collaborative and WFH is a widely appreciated option amongst colleagues especially those we are carers for elderly parents and children.
cons: Google the HSBC share price chart vs other peer universal banks and you’ll get a good idea of how well the place in general is being run. When reviewing an organization, weigh negative reviews more heavily because these often highlight the cracks and you can make a decision on whether despite the flaws (which all orgs will have) if you’d still be willing to join. Lack of accountability and ownership a recurring and persistent theme: There is a lack of accountability and ownership in general across the org where there is a culture of friends recruiting friends and hence leadership ends up mostly incapable, unimaginative and resistance to change. Talent Management is a lip service concept with poor talent tracking and development. Hence, it’s a common occurance to witness the most capable talents who focus on their work and not politics being squeezed out across the organization. Top management is well aware of this toxic aspect of the culture and trying to change it, but have not yet been successful because the ones left standing in Middle Mangement are part of the problem and hence this is a vicious negative cycle. It’s ridiculous to expect the problem to sort itself out. There are good and capable people who are unable to speak up because most parts of the bank does not have mandatory 360 feedback incorporated into the annual performance appraisal process. Hence, few (if any) are going to speak up on issues on or with their line management for fear of retribution, which is a real concern and happens often. When the power balance is so clearly tiled in favour of the line manager, they end up being the judge, jury and executioner when it comes to pay increments, bonus and even development opportunities. Performance calibration is often the argued control for this, but if the line manager is problematic to begin with, the presented perception and represention of the talent will be biased. So calibration is just a “feel good” where management pretends there is some form of check and balance to their power. But in reality is highly subjective and just a bunch of managers chatting about how much bonus they feel each talent deserves at year end. Uncompetitive Basic Salary: HSBC should really stop using the word “competitive” in their hiring ads. Because it’s well known in the industry that they underpay 15-50% below market average (depending on which business you are in). Most HSBC lifers know this and tell new joiners that the significantly lower pay is compensated by the very generous benefits package (which includes staff home loan rates, children educational grants etc). However, these benefits are not applicable for people who rent and have no children. Plus with the steep inflationary environment, staff can’t use these to offset normal daily increasing expenses like food, utilites and transport etc. We can’t eat our benefits. Who should work at HSBC: Essentially, those we are talented, capable, innovative and want a dynamic career will be ill-suited for HSBC as you’ll find yourself in an uncondusive environment which does not recognize nor pay well in return. It’s better suited for retirees or professional in their last leg of their career before retiring.They will find the work culture and environment a better fit given the repetitive job nature, little or slow change and lack of personal development. It will likely feel like a comfortable fit.
